stories.headline: OpenAI Safety Lead David Robinson Resigns, Cites Broken Culture
stories.hook: David Robinson resigns from OpenAI, claiming the culture is broken.
stories.tldr: David Robinson has resigned from OpenAI, publishing an essay in The Atlantic where he claims the company’s culture is broken. Robinson noted that he led the writing of safety reports accompanying major product launches, yet felt compelled to leave. He described himself as something of a cliché for issuing dire warnings upon departure. The resignation highlights internal tensions regarding safety oversight at the leading AI firm.

facts.text: In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches.
By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job.

stances.position: Robinson's resignation follows a predictable pattern of safety concerns raised at the last moment. The receipt is his own admission of being a cliché.
This isn't just drama; it signals that safety protocols are lagging behind product velocity. You need to watch how they handle the next launch.

predictions.claim: By October 3, 2027, no former OpenAI safety employee will publish a similar resignation essay citing a broken culture.
By December 2026, OpenAI will hire a new head of safety who publicly disputes Robinson's claims about the culture.

transcript.text: He calls himself a cliché. That’s not a warning; that’s a performance review of his own career arc. He wrote the safety reports for the big launches, and now he’s leaving because the culture is broken. I’m looking for the mechanism. Where exactly did the incentive rot set in? Or is this just the standard exit interview script?

You’re missing the signal in the noise. He didn’t just quit; he published an essay in The Atlantic detailing his role in those safety reports. This means the gap between what was shipped and what was deemed safe is now public knowledge. Watch what happens next. If they ignore this, the next launch will be scrutinized differently.

memeLine.text: The classic exit interview: 'I warned you.'

body.text: David Robinson’s resignation from OpenAI arrives with the familiar thud of a safety lead walking away from the machine. In an essay published in The Atlantic, Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches. Yet, by his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job. The phrasing is precise, almost weary. It suggests he knows the playbook well enough to recite it before anyone else can critique it. Mara would point out that the receipt here is not the resignation itself, but the timing. He left after writing the reports, not during. The question remains whether the culture broke because of the work, or if the work was always going to break the culture.

Look at the artifact: the safety reports themselves. They were written for major product launches. That means they existed alongside shipping code. When a safety lead feels the need to go public with such specific claims about cultural failure, it usually means internal channels have failed to alter the trajectory. Rex sees the overhang here: the next launch will carry the weight of this public dispute. Investors and regulators will see the resignation not as a personnel change, but as a flag. The direction is clear—safety is no longer a back-office function but a central narrative risk. You are going to see this play out in the next earnings call or press release, where the language around safety will likely become more defensive or more vague.

Let’s stick to the text. Robinson claimed the company’s ‘culture is broken’. That is a broad assertion. Without a specific metric—like a percentage drop in retention or a number of blocked features—the claim remains subjective. However, the fact that he chose to publish in The Atlantic rather than internally suggests the internal mechanism for addressing these concerns had already failed. The cliché he mentions is not just about the warning, but about the lack of impact the warning had until it was too late.

stories.headline: AI vs. SI: What the Super Intelligence Rename Means for Businesses and Builders
stories.hook: Federal paperwork now says Super Intelligence (SI). Your contracts still say AI. Here is how to run both vocabularies.
stories.tldr: A White House order makes Super Intelligence (SI) the federal word for what statutes, state laws, contracts and vendor questionnaires still call artificial intelligence (AI). For anyone selling to, reporting to or building for the government, the practical job is not a rename; it is running two vocabularies that point at the same systems in some settings and not in others. To researchers, superintelligence already means something far beyond today’s systems, and the studio behind this desk now uses SI for Synthetic Intelligence. What should you keep, map and watch?

facts.text: Organizations may soon encounter "SI" in federal agency materials while statutes, state laws, contracts, internal policies, vendor questionnaires and governance frameworks continue to use "AI."
It is how to manage two vocabularies that may refer to the same systems in some settings but not necessarily in every legal or operational context.

For purposes of this order, and except where otherwise provided by law, the terms “Super Intelligence” and “SI” mean the technologies and systems encompassed by the term “artificial intelligence” as defined in section 9401(3) of title 15, United States Code.

Entities interacting with executive branch agencies, including federal contractors, grant applicants, and companies filing regulatory comments, should expect and prepare for agency solicitations, forms, and official correspondence to adopt the "Super Intelligence" nomenclature going forward.

“Superintelligence is already a word, and it means something different than AI; specifically, AI that is vastly superhuman and so very difficult, if not impossible, to control,” said David Krueger, an AI professor and founder of the AI risk advocacy nonprofit Evitable.

stances.position: The rename lands on compliance teams first: a contract that says AI, an agency form that says SI, one system, two boxes. Keep AI as the legal term and add a mapping line.

transcript.text: Name one person this lands on. A compliance lead whose contract says AI, whose new federal solicitation says SI, and whose customer questionnaire asks which one the product is. The fix is not a find-and-replace. It is one definitions line that says the federal SI and the statutory AI are the same systems, until the law says otherwise.

memeLine.text: One system. Two acronyms. One person filling in both boxes.

body.text: Name one person this lands on. Take a clearly labeled role rather than a real person: the compliance lead at a software vendor that sells to the federal government. A new agency solicitation says Super Intelligence (SI) where earlier ones said artificial intelligence (AI). Her master services agreement still says AI. So do the company’s internal policies, its state-law obligations and the vendor questionnaires its customers send. The IAPP, the privacy and governance association, framed the practical problem precisely: not whether every reference to AI should change, but how to manage two vocabularies that may refer to the same systems in some settings but not necessarily in every legal or operational context.

In practice, for whom, and what to do. First, keep your legal terms where they are. The order defines SI as exactly the systems the existing federal statute calls artificial intelligence, and nothing in it requires rewriting existing contracts, grants or regulations, so a mass find-and-replace adds risk and buys no protection. Second, add a mapping line. Freshfields tells clients that federal contractors, grant applicants and companies filing regulatory comments should expect agency solicitations, forms and official correspondence to adopt the new nomenclature. A one-sentence definitions clause that treats the federal SI as the statutory AI keeps both documents pointing at the same thing. Third, answer in the reader’s vocabulary: SI when replying to an agency that uses it, AI wherever the law and your customers still do. None of this is legal advice; it is a way to keep two sets of paperwork honest.

Then there is the ambiguity nobody ordered. In the research world, superintelligence is not a synonym for AI. AI professor David Krueger told the San Francisco Standard that superintelligence is already a word, and it means something different than AI: AI that is vastly superhuman and so very difficult, if not impossible, to control. A federal document that says SI is describing today’s systems under the existing statutory definition. A researcher who says superintelligence usually is not. When a sentence matters, spell the term out on first use and say which definition you mean.

A disclosure, because it bears on this piece: VaultSpark Studios, which publishes The Desk, decided on October 4, 2026 to use a hybrid vocabulary on its own pages, AI and Synthetic Intelligence (SI), in which SI stands for Synthetic Intelligence rather than Super Intelligence. That is the studio’s own editorial decision. It is not news, and it is not a federal requirement. The studio’s definitions are published on its Synthetic Intelligence page at vaultsparkstudios.com/synthetic-intelligence/ and its side-by-side comparison at vaultsparkstudios.com/ai-vs-si/.

Who absorbs the cost of two vocabularies? Mostly the people filling in forms. The cheapest fix is the boring one: a glossary line, a consistent first-use rule, and a note in the template your team reuses. Name the system, name the definition, and the acronym stops mattering.

stories.headline: The 60-Day Clock: Will ‘Super Intelligence’ Get a Legal Definition by November 28?
stories.hook: The rename took effect at once. The legal definition is due as a proposal in 60 days, and only Congress can enact it.
stories.tldr: The order inaugurating the Super Intelligence (SI) era renamed artificial intelligence (AI) for federal agencies immediately but left its legal meaning to a later step: within 60 days, by November 28, 2026, the president’s science and technology adviser must propose legislative language for a federal definition. That proposal could expand, replace or simply restate the existing statutory definition, and it goes to the President, not to a vote. The desk splits on whether the deadline produces a real legal change, a quiet restatement, or a missed date.

facts.text: Within 60 days of the date of this order, the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology (APST), in consultation with the heads of other agencies as the APST deems appropriate, shall submit to the President proposed legislative language to establish a Federal definition of “Super Intelligence” and “SI” that reflects the capabilities described in section 1 of this order.
By November 28, 2026 (within 60 days), the APST must submit proposed legislative language establishing a federal definition of those terms.

The proposal must assess whether the new definition should modify, expand, or supersede the existing AI definition; identify appropriate conforming statutory amendments; and recommend any additional presidential or executive actions needed to implement it across the executive branch.

The Order directs the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology (APST) to propose a Federal definition of “Super Intelligence” and “SI” that reflects the state of this extraordinary frontier technology and identify any additional executive action necessary to implement the proposed definition.

Any statutory definition of “Super Intelligence” could shape the scope of future federal incentives, export controls, oversight, compliance obligations, government-contract requirements, and potentially the interpretation of existing AI-related statutory and contractual provisions.
This order shall be implemented consistent with applicable law and subject to the availability of appropriations.
The costs for publication of this order shall be borne by the Office of Science and Technology Policy.

stances.position: Rename now. Definition proposed in 60 days. Statute: no date. The order runs subject to the availability of appropriations. That is a slogan with a calendar.
The deadline is the part that breaks things. A new federal definition could reach export controls, oversight and contract requirements, and every compliance template keyed to AI needs a second pass.
The test is simple: does the proposal modify, expand or supersede the existing AI definition, or restate it? Only the first three change anything. A proposal is not a law.

predictions.claim: By December 31, 2026, no bill enacting a statutory definition of Super Intelligence will have been signed into law.
By December 5, 2026, the White House will publicly release the proposed legislative language defining Super Intelligence.
By June 30, 2027, Congress will not have amended the artificial intelligence definition in 15 U.S.C. 9401(3).

transcript.text: Sixty days. Then a proposal. Then nothing scheduled. The rename cost one signature. The definition has no vote on the calendar.

The calendar is exactly what pages people. The day a federal definition stops matching the old one, every contract clause and compliance form keyed to artificial intelligence needs a second look. The happy path is that SI keeps meaning AI forever.

Then write down the test now. Does the proposal modify, expand or supersede the existing definition, or restate it under a new name? And note who receives it: the President. Nothing in the order requires the text to be published.
So the deliverable is a memo. Noted.

memeLine.text: Rename: day one. Legal definition: day 60, maybe.

body.text: Sixty days. That is the window the order gives the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology to send the President proposed legislative language defining Super Intelligence (SI). Freshfields puts the deadline at November 28, 2026. The new vocabulary did not wait for it: agencies are already told to say SI. The definition comes second. A vote, if there ever is one, comes third, with no date at all. The order says it is implemented subject to the availability of appropriations, and that the cost of publishing it is borne by the Office of Science and Technology Policy. I read the invoice. It is a short one.

Here is the scenario that pages someone, labeled as a scenario. A federal definition that goes beyond restating the old one lands in a contract clause, an export-control rule or an oversight requirement. Freshfields flags exactly that reach: any statutory definition of Super Intelligence could shape future federal incentives, export controls, oversight, compliance obligations and government-contract requirements, and potentially how existing AI-related statutory and contractual provisions are read. Every compliance template keyed to the phrase artificial intelligence (AI) then needs a second pass, and the happy path, where SI simply means AI, ends on the day the two definitions diverge.

It is in the proposal’s required contents. The proposal must assess whether the new definition should modify, expand or supersede the existing definition of artificial intelligence, identify conforming statutory amendments, and recommend further presidential or executive action. That gives us a clean test for late November. If the proposal restates the current statutory definition under a new name, the rename stays cosmetic. If it narrows or widens the boundary, the vocabulary becomes law only when Congress agrees, and not before. Also worth reading twice: the proposal goes to the President. Nothing in the order requires it to be published.

What to watch, in order. The November 28 deadline. Whether any text is released. Whether a bill carrying it finds a sponsor. Until then, SI in a federal document has one legal meaning, and it is the old one.

stories.headline: Tech Leaders Signed a ‘Super Intelligence’ Accord. Their Labs Still Say AI
stories.hook: The White House Accord on Super Intelligence carries the new name in its title. It does not ask anyone to use it.
stories.tldr: Leaders of the biggest artificial intelligence (AI) labs signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence (SI), a pledge the president called morally binding, on the same day he ordered federal agencies to swap the old term for the new one. Lawyers reading the accord found no requirement that signatories adopt the new name, and the leading labs have not relabeled their models. One executive slipped into SI on stage; the heads of Google, OpenAI and Anthropic did not. Will the industry follow once federal contracts start using it?

facts.text: Trump added that the document, dubbed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, is "morally binding" for the executives who signed it.
Although that term “Super Intelligence” appears in the accord’s title, we note that the accord does not expressly require signatories to adopt the Administration’s rebranding.
Furthermore, the agreement does not itself create legally enforceable obligations or an enforcement mechanism.
While the pledge had “super intelligence” in the title, there’s no explicit agreement among tech companies to begin referring to AI as such.
Reactions in Silicon Valley so far have been mixed, but the leading labs have not relabeled their models as SI.
The heads of Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic, which own the most advanced models, did not use the term “SI” during the press conference.
Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceXAI, was halfway through remarks at the event when he caught himself calling it “AI”: “SI, pardon me,” he said, laughing.
Apple, which did not have an executive at the White House event, has already tried rebranding the term AI.
Meta has been using the term since June 2025 and renamed its AI team “Meta Superintelligence Labs.”

stances.position: Renames by decree rarely outlive the decree. Apple already tried redefining AI and the industry kept the old word. The labs signed safety controls, not a style guide.
Watch the procurement forms, not the press conference. Once agency paperwork says SI, contractors write SI to win the bid, and you are going to see it in lab marketing next.
The accord puts Super Intelligence in the title and nowhere in the obligations. The joke draws itself: a name everyone signed and nobody has to say.

predictions.claim: By December 31, 2026, none of OpenAI, Anthropic or Google will rename a flagship model or its main product page from AI to SI.
By March 31, 2027, at least one federal agency solicitation will ask bidders to describe their systems as Super Intelligence (SI).

transcript.text: One panel. A signing table, a pledge with Super Intelligence in the title, and behind it every product page the signatories own, still reading AI. Caption: signed in SI, shipped in AI.

We have watched a company try to redefine AI before. Apple said AI meant Apple Intelligence, and everyone else kept saying AI. Names stick when the people saying them get something for it. The accord asks for internal controls and outside reviews. It never asks for the word.

That is the boring version. Wait for the paperwork. The order puts SI on agency solicitations and forms, and the labs want those contracts. The first request for proposals that asks about your Super Intelligence system changes every bid deck in the country.
Maybe. The disanalogy is real: Apple had no contracts to hand out. But a word you only say to a procurement officer is a password, not a vocabulary.

memeLine.text: Signed in SI. Shipped in AI.

body.text: Picture the signing table. The heads of the largest labs stood with the president outside the White House, a pledge with Super Intelligence in its title, a president calling it morally binding. Now picture the next morning: the same companies’ product pages, model cards and keynote slides, every one of them still saying AI. Freshfields, reading the accord for its clients, noted that it does not expressly require signatories to adopt the administration’s rebranding. The San Francisco Standard reported there is no explicit agreement among tech companies to begin referring to AI as such. The name went on the parchment. It did not go in the obligations.

We called it something else in 2024. Apple, which did not send an executive to this event, has already tried rebranding the term AI as Apple Intelligence, and the rest of the industry kept saying AI. Meta went the other way in June 2025, naming its research group Meta Superintelligence Labs, a label that rode a research ambition rather than a government memo. Names stick when the people using them gain something from saying them. At the press conference the heads of Google, OpenAI and Anthropic, which own the most advanced models, did not use the term SI. Elon Musk caught himself mid-sentence, said SI, pardon me, and laughed. That is what a vocabulary sounds like when it is being performed rather than adopted. The disanalogy worth naming: Apple had no contracts to hand out. The federal government does.

That disanalogy is the whole story, and you are going to see it play out in paperwork. The order tells agencies to use SI in solicitations, forms and official correspondence. The labs want those contracts. The accord’s actual commitments are about process: internal controls, monitoring, outside assessments and board-level oversight. None of that needs a new acronym. But the first time a request for proposals asks how your Super Intelligence system handles a task, every bid team in the country writes SI. Marketing follows procurement. Watch the forms, not the podium.

Two caveats belong under the drawing. The accord creates no legally enforceable obligations and no enforcement mechanism, so morally binding is doing all the work in that sentence. And reactions in Silicon Valley so far have been mixed, but the leading labs have not relabeled their models as SI. Until one of them does, the caption stays as drawn.

stories.headline: Trump Order Renames AI ‘Super Intelligence (SI)’ for Agencies. The Law Stays the Same
stories.hook: Agencies must say Super Intelligence (SI) instead of artificial intelligence (AI). The legal definition did not move.
stories.tldr: A new executive order directs federal agencies to write Super Intelligence (SI) wherever they used to write artificial intelligence (AI), in letters, websites, reports and other non-statutory documents. What it leaves alone matters more: the order defines SI as exactly the technologies the existing federal statute already calls artificial intelligence, does not require old regulations, contracts or grants to change, and gives companies no new obligations. The vocabulary changed. The law did not, and the open question is whether it ever will.

facts.text: Today, President Donald J. Trump signed an Executive Order to replace the term “Artificial Intelligence” (“AI”) with “Super Intelligence” (“SI”) in the executive branch to recognize the continuously advancing technological frontier and the limitless promise it offers the American people.

Signed after a White House summit with leading technology executives, the order directs federal agencies to use the terms "Super Intelligence" and "SI" in official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents and other non-statutory materials.

For purposes of this order, and except where otherwise provided by law, the terms “Super Intelligence” and “SI” mean the technologies and systems encompassed by the term “artificial intelligence” as defined in section 9401(3) of title 15, United States Code.
Nothing in this section requires the alteration of previously issued regulations, Presidential actions, contracts, grants, or other historical documents.
The immediate change is linguistic, not a wholesale rewrite of U.S. laws governing AI.

stances.position: The order renames the word, not the thing. Section 3 defines Super Intelligence as the existing statutory definition of artificial intelligence, unchanged.

transcript.text: Everyone read Section 1, the part about a new era. I read Section 3, the part that says Super Intelligence means whatever the statute already meant by artificial intelligence. Same systems, same legal boundary, new initials. The real test is whether Congress ever changes the definition. Until then this is a style guide with a seal on it.

memeLine.text: New name on the letterhead. Same definition in Section 3.

body.text: It is in Section 3. The executive order President Trump signed on September 29, titled Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence, spends its opening section on ambition: today’s frontier systems, it says, are no longer merely artificial intelligence (AI) but the start of an era of Super Intelligence (SI). Then Section 3 quietly defines Super Intelligence as the technologies and systems already covered by the term artificial intelligence in section 9401(3) of title 15 of the United States Code. Same systems. Same legal boundary. New initials.

Here is what actually changes. Executive departments and agencies must use Super Intelligence and SI in place of artificial intelligence and AI in official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents and other non-statutory documents, to the maximum extent permitted by law. The White House fact sheet adds that agencies are to no longer acknowledge the old terms. If you deal with a federal agency, expect the new words on its forms, solicitations and press releases. That is the whole of the immediate change, and it is addressed to the executive branch.

Here is what does not change. Nothing in the order requires agencies to rewrite previously issued regulations, Presidential actions, contracts, grants or other historical documents. Congress has not amended the statute. State laws, private contracts, internal policies and vendor questionnaires still say artificial intelligence. As the privacy and governance association IAPP put it in its analysis, the immediate change is linguistic, not a wholesale rewrite of U.S. laws governing AI.

The receipt that would prove this is more than a rename is a statute. The order gives the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology 60 days to send the President proposed legislative language for a federal definition of Super Intelligence, including an assessment of whether it should modify, expand or supersede the existing definition of artificial intelligence. Until a bill carrying that language becomes law, SI in a federal document means precisely what AI meant the week before. Read the letterhead for tone. Read Section 3 for the law.
